My name is Alexey Grudin, and I've spent the last few years at the epicenter of a storm called “team leadership” My journey: 🔥 Team Lead in BigTech AI Product Management Software Development What Companies Gain and Lose by Implementing AI: A 3–5 Year Horizon Alex Grudin 7 min read · Just now -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size AI lowers the cost of production. It raises the cost of trust, verification, and meaning. Most discussions of AI adoption in companies focus on development productivity. The usual questions are: How much faster is code written? How much more often do releases happen? How many engineers can be replaced? How much is time-to-market reduced? However, this view is too narrow. AI affects not only development. It gradually penetrates the entire value-creation loop: Understanding the market ↓ Idea generation ↓ Prioritization ↓ Requirements formulation ↓ Development ↓ Testing ↓ Release ↓ Analysis of results ↓ Next decision Therefore, the main question of the coming years sounds different: What does an organization gain thanks to AI, and what may it lose in the process? Where Companies Will Almost Certainly Win 1. The cost of producing knowledge and artifacts will fall sharply AI reduces the cost of almost any intellectual work: data analysis; preparing research; writing requirements; generating hypotheses; creating documentation; writing code; testing; preparing reports. The number of produced artifacts will grow faster than ever before. Organizations will be able to test more hypotheses and launch more initiatives with the same resources. 2. The speed of delivering changes will increase The most noticeable effect will be seen in operations. Companies will be able to: launch experiments faster; create prototypes faster; implement features faster; fix bugs faster. At the level of individual tasks, the productivity gain may be very significant. 3. The threshold for creating new products will fall Many tasks that previously required an entire team of specialists will become available to small groups. There will be more: startups; niche products; internal initiatives; product experiments. The cost of validating an idea will continue to fall. 4. The culture of experimentation will strengthen Historically, most companies suffered from a lack of testable hypotheses. AI makes experiments cheap. Organizations will be able to make decisions based on a larger number of tests, not only expert opinions. Where Companies May Lose 1. Overproduction of solutions and attention deficit Historically, the constraint on business was a lack of ideas. Now the constraint becomes the ability to choose among them. The organization begins to produce: more hypotheses; more research; more features; more experiments; more changes. But the ability to understand which of them really matter grows much more slowly. The problem becomes not a shortage of solutions but a shortage of attention. AI easily generates dozens of options, but selection and interpretation still require human judgment. The rarest resource becomes not the idea but the ability to understand which one makes sense. 2. Over-generation of ideas and loss of meaning This risk deserves a separate discussion, because it has manifested earlier than expected. AI systems tend toward homogenization: in brainstorming they gravitate toward average, predictable solutions, and the collective diversity of ideas falls even when individual ideas seem more creative. Studies record the effect of cultural stagnation: generative systems compress meaning toward the most familiar and easily reproducible rather than creating the new. A paradox arises. The more ideas are produced, the less meaning each individual idea has. Ideas cease to be value — they become noise. An organization that previously suffered from a shortage of hypotheses now suffers from their excess without selection criteria. The loss of meaning and values occurs not at the level of an individual artifact but at the level of the entire decision-making system. When AI proposes the next step, implements it, and analyzes the result, the organization has fewer and fewer reasons to independently build causal models of its business. Formally, a human confirms the decision. In fact, the meaning of the decision belongs less and less to anyone. This is over-generation of ideas in its worst manifestation: not when there are no ideas, but when there are too many, and none of them is rooted in understanding. 3. Development as a bottleneck Here one must be precise. Development has become a bottleneck not because AI writes code poorly. On the contrary — code is written faster than ever. Development has become a bottleneck because the rest of the loop cannot keep up with it.
